newsitem.title: USA: Wis. board slips through sale of stadium bonds.
newsitem.headline: Wis. board slips through sale of stadium bonds.

text.p: A Wisconsin board charged with financing a $250 million ballpark for the Milwaukee Brewers baseball team quietly sold $146.7 million of convertible option bonds Wednesday.

The deal, which was originally envisioned as a long-term sales tax revenue bond issue, was instead structured as convertible option bonds that gives the Southeast Wisconsin Professional Baseball Park District board the ability to force a tender of the bonds anytime between March 1 and December 15, 1997.

The bonds were sold at an interest rate of 4.10 percent, according to Bear, Stearns & Co, the senior manager for the deal. The bonds were awarded by the board at a meeting Thursday morning in West Allis, Wis.
The sale was blasted Thursday by the head of a taxpayers group challenging the constitutionality of a 0.1 percent, five-county sales tax backing the bonds.
"I take this as a slap in the face of constitutional government," said George Watts. "It's a temporary victory of greed over freedom."

Watts said the sale would not deter the group from pressing on with a lawsuit, currently pending before the U.S. Court of Appeal in Chicago. The suit had been dismissed by a federal court judge in Milwaukee and the constitutionality of the tax has been upheld by the Wisconsin Supreme Court.

Watts said the sale may end up circumventing plans to file a lawsuit in Wisconsin state court challenging the bonds. He added the group may soon bring up some environmental concerns about the stadium site.
Details on why the bond issue was structured as convertible bonds were not available from board representatives or from firms involved in the deal.

The deal was rated only by Moody's Investors Service, which assigned a MIG1 rating based on the strength of the escrow agreement, which calls for all the bond proceeds to be placed into a guarenteed investment contract provided by triple-A rated Bayerische Landesanstalt. The GIC is expected to provide enough interest to make interest payments on the bonds until their tender.

According to Moody's, the bonds will be redeemed or restructured as long-term, fixed-rate bonds following the tender. Up until then, no proceeds from the issue can be expended for the stadium project or even for issuance costs, Moody's said.
A Moody's analyst has said the MIG1 rating does not "speak to the credit quality of the (baseball) district" or address the lawsuit.

The analyst also said the issue was structured to deal with the pending litigation and concerns about the reintroduction of a bill in January by U.S. Sen. Patrick Moynihan that would ban the use of tax-exempt bonds for professional sports stadiums. That bill is expected to include a retroactive date for stadium deals.
